DECISION ON
VUKELICH

HEARING

OF THE

HONOURABLE JUDGE A.L.
ORMISTON

Counsel for the Crown:

D. Williams, M.
Rankin

Counsel for the Defendant:

P. Jaffe

Place of Hearing:

Abbotsford
, B.C.

Date of Hearing:

March 6, 7, 8, and 9,
2023

Date of Judgment:

April 20, 2023

[
1
]

I will begin by repeating Court of Appeal’s concluding
remarks in
Beaudoin v. British Columbia

2022 BCCA 427
, because they help
situate the issues at the centre of this hearing:

“The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted our
interdependence as a community. It forced us to confront the reality that the
pursuit of some activities, including the exercise of some constitutionally
protected rights, would increase the risk of exponential spread of the disease
and the loss of human life. In the exercise of her responsibility to safeguard
public health and access to our healthcare system, the [Provincial Health
Officer] made time-limited and setting-specific orders restricting activities
she considered to be most likely to foster widespread transmission of the
virus. She was uniquely qualified to make these decisions and the exercise of
her judgment must be afforded deference (at para 307).”

[…]

“As Justice La Forest put it in
Ross v. New Brunswick School
District No. 15
,
[1996] 1 S.C.R. 825
at para.

72
,
1996 CanLII 237
, "... freedom of religion ensures that every
individual must be free to hold and to manifest without State interference
those beliefs and opinions dictated by one's conscience... [but it] is subject
to such limitations as are necessary to promote public safety, order, health
... and the fundamental rights and freedoms of others."  This is one of
those cases (at para 310).”

[
2
]

There are 19 tickets before this court and they
were issued for alleged violations of Gathering and Events Orders
[i]
(‘the Orders’) made by the
Provincial Health Officer (‘PHO’) in response to the Covid-19 pandemic.  These
Orders were issued by the PHO under authority law makers have granted to her in
the
Public Health Act
(‘PHA’).

[
3
]

Each of the accused (‘the
Applicants’) has given notice of their intention to challenge the
constitutional validity of the Orders under which they were charged.  All
assert that the limitation on their right to worship in person are breaches
under
ss.2(a)
(b)(c)(d),
7
, and
15(1)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
(‘the
Charter’
).  They will argue that the Crown cannot
justify the Orders under s.1, and if successful will ultimately ask this court
to dismiss the charges against them.
[ii]

[
4
]

The following are my
reasons on the Crown’s motion to summarily dismiss the
Charter

applications on all tickets without the necessity of holding a full evidentiary
hearing.  Before I begin, I will say a few words about the context of this
decision.  A trial has been conducted on one of the tickets
[iii]
and I found Pastor Koopman
hosted an event contrary to a Gathering & Events Order on December 6,
2020.  Evidence has not been heard on trials for the remaining tickets.  Counsel
have since consented to this
Vukelich
hearing being conducted together
for all of the separate tickets.

[
5
]

The first of the
Applicants’ Notices of Constitutional Question was filed in May 2021 and the
Crown responded with its notice seeking a
Vukelich
hearing in July of
the same year.  It has been a long road to arrive at this point.  In the
interim the Applicants have given notice of a s.11(b) application to dismiss
the charges on the basis of unreasonable delay.  They also announced an
intention during the
Vukelich
hearing to bring applications related to
abuse of process, and formal notice was indeed filed earlier this month.  The
delay and abuse of process applications were not part of the earlier
Charter

applications and are not subject to this ruling today.

The Law

[
6
]

This Court’s power to
screen constitutional applications for merit is
established in
R. v.
Vukelich

(1996),
1996 CanLII 1005 (BC CA)
,
108 C.C.C.(3d)193 (B.C.C.A.)
.  While the
Vukelich

case
deals specifically with applications to exclude evidence, courts have
since ruled on the broader scope of such hearings.
In
R. v. Cody

2017
SCC 31
, in the context of the Court’s obligation to minimize delay, the Supreme
Court of Canada confirmed that trial judges can dismiss an application when it
has no “reasonable prospect of success” and there is “no basis upon which the
application could succeed.”
Vukelich
hearings have also been extended
to cases where the remedy sought is something other than the exclusion of
evidence, including an application for a stay of proceedings or challenges to
legislation (
Trans Mountain Pipeline ULC v. Mivasair
,
2020 BCCA 255
at
para
50
).

[
7
]

While it is the Crown
that requested a
Vukelich
hearing, the question this Court has to answer
is whether the
Charter
Applicants have shown a reasonable prospect of
success in obtaining the sought after remedy (
R. v. Frederickson
,
2018
BCCA 2
at para
26
,
Trans Mountain Pipeline ULC v. Mivasair
at para
52
).

[
8
]

The Applicants have at
times characterized this
Vukelich
hearing as an attempt to suppress
legitimate legal and factual disputes.  It is important to note that a
Vukelich

hearing does not prevent the advancement of facts or law, quite the opposite.
It is the Applicant’s opportunity to show the court what facts it would lead at
a full evidentiary hearing, and moreover, the court must assume those facts to
be true for the purposes of the
Vukelich
analysis.
The question to be
answered on this hearing is whether the facts being advanced by the Applicants
disclose a basis in law for the remedy being sought.

The Issues

[
9
]

The Crown presents
several reasons to summarily dismiss the defence applications.  At the risk of
oversimplifying their argument, the Crown says that the
Charter
applications
cannot be brought now, and they cannot be brought here. They cannot be brought
‘now,’ that being at the trial stage, because allowing the Applicants to
‘breach first and challenge later’ would allow an impermissible collateral
attack on Orders that were meant to address a public health emergency back in
2020 and 2021.  They cannot be brought ‘here’ because to grant their
applications would be inconsistent with appellate precedent that can only be
challenged in the Supreme Court of Canada.

[
10
]

Underpinning the Applicants’ submission is one
theme: a summary dismissal of these
Charter
challenges would unjustly
deny a remedy for breaches of their fundamental rights and the ability to defend
themselves on the charges before the court.

For understandable reasons,
the submissions of the Applicants are passionate given the significant rights
that were suspended during these temporary Orders.  It bears repeating that
for more than three days this court heard comprehensive
argument about the law and how it applies to the facts the Applicants would
lead on a full evidentiary hearing.  The Applicants have not been at all
constrained in what they have put before this Court and they have had more than
a year to marshal the evidence they intend to raise in their
Charter

applications.

[
11
]

For these specific Applicants, who have made clear through counsel
that they fear being ignored and unheard, I will say that I have deliberated
carefully over counsel’s submissions and the vast record that has been filed.  More
importantly, four of the six Applicants before me were parties to proceedings
in
Beaudoin v. British
Columbia
2021 BCSC 512
,
affirmed
2022 BCCA 427
,
a case that is at the centre of
legal arguments before this Court.  Their pressing constitutional concerns about
public health orders limiting rights to in person worship were heard in a
stunningly swift time under judicial review by the Chief Justice of the British
Columbia Supreme Court.  This took place in the early days of a global pandemic
that had many citizens and litigants waiting on the side-lines.  The Court in
Beaudoin

recognized the rights being infringed were significant.  The Court also
recognized that in November 2020 when the prohibitions on in person worship began,
the PHO was attempting to address the risk of accelerated transmission of
Covid-19, protecting the vulnerable and maintaining the integrity of the health
care system.  Her Orders were made in the face of significant uncertainty and
required highly specialized medical and scientific expertise (
Beaudoin
BCSC,
para 244).

[
12
]

The Court of Appeal has gone on to review and uphold the
constitutionality of these Orders.  In both levels of court, justices showed a determined
commitment to respond to the grievances before them.  Procedural rules were
applied with flexibility to allow the courts to answer the precise questions
being asked by the petitioners.  For example, the original Orders were reviewed
as opposed to reconsideration decisions; and in deciding whether the
infringements of rights were justifiable in a free and democratic society the
Court of Appeal undertook the
Oakes
analysis, even though the Court
found that the correct test was the one articulated in
Doré
.

[
13
]

The applications before me raise identical challenges to the
Orders.  For reasons I will go through in detail now, I will summarily dismiss
the
Charter
applications subject to this
Vukelich
application.  This
ruling does not deprive the Applicants of their ability to challenge the
charges against them.  They are (on all but one) presumed innocent and will
have trial dates set.  What this ruling confirms is that one of the grounds the
Applicants would advance, that is the constitutional validity of the Orders
under which they are charged, has already been heard and decided by the highest
court in this province.

Summary of Positions
on Collateral Attack

[
14
]

The first of the Crown’s
arguments regarding the collateral attack rule was recently ruled upon
in
R.
v. Lucier

2022 BCPC 191
.
In
Lucier
the accused had given notice of the
same
Charter
challenges to a Gathering and Events Order.  The Court
agreed with the Crown that such challenges were an impermissible collateral
attack on an administrative Order, and summarily dismissed the
Charter

applications.

[
15
]

Crown submits the cases
at bar are indistinguishable from
Lucier
and that horizontal
stare
decisis
binds this Court.  The Applicants dis
agree with the analysis in
Lucier
,
disagree that it is in any way determinative of matters before this Court, and
submit that
Lucier
is factually distinguishable.

Summary of Positions
on Legal Viability

[
16
]

If the Crown’s
collateral attack argument fails and we embark on the evidentiary hearing the
Applicants seek, Crown submits this Court would be bound by the decision in
Beaudoin
,
wherein the same Orders withstood constitutional challenge on the same grounds.
Crown further submits that in similar constitutional challenges to similar
Orders across the country, there is not one case in support of the Applicants’
position.

[
17
]

As I have mentioned,
some of the petitioners in
Beaudoin
are also Applicants before me, and
they are: John Koopman, Brent Smith, Riverside Calvary Chapel, and Immanuel
Covenant Reformed Church.  The other two Applicants on these tickets, Timothy
Champ and James Butler, were not petitioners in
Beaudoin
, however they
did provide affidavits that formed part of the record in that case.  When it
comes to the nature of the alleged infringements of their
Charter

rights, the factual basis put forward by all Applicants is identical to what
was before the Courts in
Beaudoin
.  The Applicants have pointed to
additional evidence they would lead at a full evidentiary hearing before this
Court, however it relates to the legal analysis under s.1.

[
18
]

The Applicants submit
that even though several parties are the same, the additional evidence they
would lead in a
Charter
application before this Court is distinct from
Beaudoin

in significant ways.  At the heart of the Applicants’ position is the assertion
that the ruling in
Beaudoin
cannot foreclose their ability to challenge
the Orders again in this forum with a more fulsome evidentiary record,
particularly where their innocence on allegations of a quazi-criminal nature is
at stake.  The Applicants submit there is no rule against repeating
constitutional challenges when the legal landscape is in the process of being formed.

Analysis
Collateral Attack Rule

[
19
]

The Crown’s first
argument is that these
Charter
applications, brought after the
Applicants allegedly violated the PHOs orders, are an impermissible collateral
attack.  In short, Crown submits that the legislature did not intend to allow
people to challenge the validity of these public health orders at trial once
they had already been breached. Crown argues that the proper forum to challenge
the Orders is through the legislated reconsideration process in
s.43
of the
Public
Health Act
, which allows the PHO to vary or rescind Orders.  The Orders can
also be constitutionally challenged on a judicial review.  Crown takes the
position that it would be a collateral attack for the Applicants to side-step
the intended process for redress and challenge the constitutionality of the
orders after allegedly breaching them.

[
20
]

This is the precise
argument that was advanced by the Crown and accepted by the Court
in
Lucier
.

Lucier
applies
the Supreme Court of Canada formulation of the collateral
attack rule described in paragraph 21 of
R. v. Bird

2019 SCC 7
:

“A collateral
attack is an attack on an order "made in proceedings other than those
whose specific object is the reversal, variation or nullification of the
order" (Wilson v. The Queen,
1983 CanLII 35 (SCC)
, [1983] 2 S.C.R. 594, at p. 599; Canada
(Attorney General) v. TeleZone Inc.,
2010 SCC 62
, [2010] 3 S.C.R. 585, at para.

60
). This Court has recognized a general rule against collateral attacks on
court orders: with limited exceptions, an order issued by a court must be
obeyed unless it is set aside in a proceeding taken for that purpose (
Maybrun
,
at paras. 2-3;
R. v. Litchfield
,
1993 CanLII 44 (SCC)
, [1993] 4 S.C.R. 333, at p. 349;
Garland
v. Consumers' Gas Co
.,
2004 SCC 25
, [2004] 1 S.C.R. 629, at para.
71
). In
Maybrun
,
the Court held that a different analysis was warranted for collateral attacks
on administrative orders. . . .”

[
21
]

The Court in
Lucier
goes on to analyse the reconsideration
process established in s.43 of the PHA and concludes that it is clear that the
PHA allows for a review of public health orders by the PHO.  The Court again
relies on
R. v. Bird
in concluding that the appropriate legal framework to
determine whether it can rule on the validity of an administrative order
collaterally attacked in penal proceedings is established in
R. v.
Consolidated Maybrun Mines Ltd.

1998 CanLII 820 (SCC)
, [1998] 1 S.C.R. 706 (‘
Maybrun’
).

[
22
]

In applying the
Maybrun
analysis the Court in
Lucier

finds that the PHA creates a comprehensive regime for addressing a health
hazard, like Covid-19 (at para 42).  The Court finds that nothing within the
PHA suggests a legislative intention to permit a challenge to orders made
pursuant to it to be challenged in subsequent prosecutions (at para 43).  In
fact, it would undermine the purpose of the PHA if people could ignore public
health orders imposed by health officers, that were meant to address an
imminent health risk to the public, and then challenge those orders in later
proceedings (at para 45).

[
23
]

The Court did not accept Pastor Lucier’s ‘forceful’ argument that
there is no effective right of appeal to the public health orders issued under
the PHA.  The Court reviewed the reconsideration process established in s. 43
of the PHA, and while acknowledging that the process may not be as robust as
some, the Court was guided by the purpose of the legislation and intentions of
its drafters.  And then the Court stated what must be obvious to the parties
before me, that the public health orders can also be judicially reviewed.

[
24
]

Lucier
concludes the
Maybrun

analysis by finding that it was the intention of the legislature to have those
with appropriate expertise tasked with reviewing the merits of a request for
reconsideration of a public health order.  The Court of Appeal has since
emphasized in
Beaudoin
that the PHO is uniquely qualified to do just
that, whereas a court comprised of jurists is not (
Beaudoin
, BCCA at
para 209).  In considering the nature of the penalty on a conviction for
failing to comply with the Order in question, which is a fine, the Court again
concludes that it was the legislature’s intention not to allow a collateral
attack.  After weighing all of the
Maybrun
factors, the Court ruled that
Pastor Lucier’s
Charter
challenge to the public health order must be
summarily dismissed as an impermissible collateral attack.

[
25
]

The Crown submits this Court is bound by the principle of horizontal

stare decisis
to follow the decision in
Lucier
.
The Applicants submit the authorities
relied upon by Crown are either distinguishable or otherwise non-binding on
this Court.  I cannot accede to the submission that
Lucier
is not
binding on this Court.
Re Hansard Spruce Mills

1954 CanLII 253 (BC SC)
,
[1954] 4 D.L. R. 590
(B.C.S.C.)
has guided the application of horizontal
stare decisis
in
this province for almost seventy years.  These principles have recently been
affirmed by
the Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v. Sullivan

2022 SCC 19
.

[
26
]

Hansard Spruce Mills
would allow me to depart from the
Lucier

decision
if: (i) it had been undermined by subsequent appellate decisions,
which at this time, it has not, (ii) if it was made in urgent or otherwise
dynamic circumstances and was not fully considered, which it clearly was not,
or (iii) if it was reached
per incuriam
, which means through a careless
or inadvertent ignorance of binding authority.

[
27
]

On the basis of
R.
v.

Sullivan
, the Applicants submit that where the legal landscape is
being developed the principles of
stare decisis
should not stifle
development of the law.  In my view, the legal analysis
applied in
Lucier

is neither novel nor unsettled.  The decision rests firmly on law established
in appellate authorities, namely
R. v. Bird
and
Maybrun
.  What is
novel about
Lucier
is the application of these authorities to very new
public health orders, and doing so is premised on the orders being characterized
as administrative decisions as opposed to laws of general application.  This
issue too, has been completely and definitively resolved by the Court in
Beaudoin
.
The Applicants simply cannot maintain, before this Court at least, that the Orders
they are alleged to have violated are laws of general application.  Both the
B.C. Supreme Court and Court of Appeal in
Beaudoin
have unequivocally
found otherwise.

[
28
]

Ultimately, the
Applicants are really submitting that
Lucier
is wrongly decided
.
The
Supreme Court in
Sullivan
has now made clear that trial judges should
not apply subjective tests such as whether a parallel proceeding is ‘plainly
wrong’ because it leads to rulings being overturned based on judges merely disagreeing
with one another.

[
29
]

The Applicants have
framed some of their arguments under the
per incuriam
exception in
Hansard
Spuce Mills
, submitting for instance that the Court
in
Lucier
reversed
the onus in the
Maybrun
analysis.  I can see no errors in the way
Lucier

applies
the binding test established in
Maybrun
.

[
30
]

Finally, much as they
appear to have done
in
Lucier
, the Applicants have focussed their
submissions on maintaining that their substantive and procedural rights are not
protected by the reconsideration process or judicial review.  However, the
alleged flaws in the reconsideration process for these temporary emergency Orders
were argued before the Court
in
Lucier
, and before the Supreme Court and
Court of Appeal in
Beaudoin
.  The Court of Appeal in
Beaudoin

found the reconsideration process was adequate to withstand scrutiny.  I can
see no basis for this Court to find otherwise.

[
31
]

The Applicants submit
that if I accept the facts that would be alleged at a full evidentiary hearing,
I would find that all of the Applicants before this Court had no choice but to
‘breach first and challenge later’ because their requests for reconsideration
were ignored.  It is additionally submitted that I would have to find the
judicial review ineffective because it did not allow for a proper evidentiary
record to challenge the Orders.

[
32
]

A brief outline of the
timeline of events is worth reviewing here.  The prohibitions in question were first
ordered November 19, 2020.  The tickets were issued on dates between November
29, 2020 and April 2021.  The Applicants assert that members of their
congregations wrote hundreds of letters to the PHO in November and December of
2020, and some of Applicants and other religious leaders wrote to the PHO
directly.  The petitioners in
Beaudoin
, four of whom are accused on
these tickets, filed their application for judicial review on January 7 2021.
On January 29 2001 the petitioners in
Beaudoin
made a formal and
comprehensive reconsideration request resulting in a variance of the Order for
them on February 25, 2021.  March 1-3 and 5 2021 the judicial review was heard
and, somehow, comprehensively decided and written less than two weeks later on
March 18.

[
33
]

With respect to the reconsideration process, the
Applicants’ argument is premised on the conclusion, not the fact, that their
early letters sent to the PHO were requests for reconsideration as described in
s.43 of the PHA.  The evidence the Applicants have produced at this hearing
that pre-dates the January 29 2021 reconsideration request cannot be considered
applications under s.43.  Most of the correspondence before me was also before
the Court of Appeal in
Beaudoin
, and at paragraph 192 the Court finds:

“If the appellants are saying that their ability to meaningfully
engage the reconsideration process contemplated by the PHA was compromised and
did not present them with an adequate alternative remedy, that submission is
not supported by what actually occurred. Further, the PHO's response to
reconsideration requests made by non-parties are irrelevant.”

[
34
]

Section 43 may not
require a high degree of formality, but it does have basic requirements in sub
sections (1) and (2).  On my assessment, the communications from the Applicants
to the PHO are demands for the Orders to be rescinded with promises of non-compliance
instead of proposals for how to meet the objectives of the Orders that in her
qualified opinion were required to protect lives and the viability of the
public health system.  While the Applicants emphasize that they were already
taking significant steps to maintain a safe environment in their churches in
accordance with Orders from the PHO that had been in place before, this does
not take into account that in November 2020 the PHO decided that gatherings
must be prohibited as opposed to controlled.  Her decision was based on the
conclusion that measures that had been in place before were no longer
adequate.

[
35
]

A review of the
correspondence and dates of the alleged violations is not capable of supporting
the Applicants’ position that they had no choice but to save their challenges
to the Orders for trial.  For example, the tickets issued to Pastor Koopman on
December 6th and 13th 2020, and to Riverside Calvary Chapel on November 29 2020
pre-date any of their respective communications with the PHO.

[
36
]

What follows is an
exchange of correspondence that the Court of Appeal has already found were not requests
for reconsideration.  The PHO wrote to Pastor Koopman and Brent Smith directly
in December 2020 offering guidance about making a reconsideration request.  On
the basis of letters that were apparently sent by parishioners, even if the
Applicants believed they had made reconsideration requests, s. 43(6) makes
clear that an Order is not suspended during the period of reconsideration.

[
37
]

The only tickets before
me that were issued to Applicants after a proper reconsideration request or
petition for judicial review were two tickets issued to Pastor Koopman on March
7 and 12, 2021.  It is notable that these alleged violations occurred after a
reconsideration decision was granted, and s.43(5) states that after a
reconsideration decision is made, no further request for reconsideration may be
made.  On March 7 and 12, 2021 the only decision outstanding was the petition
before the Supreme Court.  These March tickets issued to Pastor Koopman came
fast on the heels of the petition being heard and before judgment was rendered
on March 18.

[
38
]

With respect to Pastors
Champ and Butler (who were not petitioners in
Beaudoin
), counsel made
inconsistent submissions about whether they had pursued reconsideration
requests.  Counsel’s position seemed to blossom into the contention that they
had made reconsideration requests that were ignored.  On the basis of letters
that have been marked as exhibits at this hearing I can see no way to draw the
conclusion Pastors Champ and Butler made any reconsideration requests at all.
The letter from counsel John Sikkema specifically lists the clients for whom he
is acting and does not appear to include Pastors Champ and Butler.  The fact
that these accused are also associated with Reformed churches is not sufficient
to say this was a request sent on their behalf.

[
39
]

As for the multitude of
letters sent by parishioners that were mentioned in submissions, I have no way
of knowing whether these are proper requests for reconsideration or expressions
of opinion regarding the Orders.  It is not clear whether they sought changes
to the Orders on behalf of Pastors Champ and Butler.  Even if it were
established that letters were sent, it is important to keep in perspective that
the relevance of whether Pastors Champ or Butler availed themselves of the
reconsideration process lies in the Applicants’ submission that the
reconsideration process cannot be found to be an effective means of reviewing
the PHOs orders.  In my view nothing that has been adduced at this
Vukelich

hearing distinguishes the efficacy of the reconsideration process for Pastors
Champ and Butler from the petitioners before the Court in
Beaudoin
.

[
40
]

All Applicants further submit
that the judicial review process has proven to be an ineffective means of
challenging the Orders.  This is impossible to reconcile with the fact that two
of the Applicants did not pursue this remedy at all, and four of them did
pursue this remedy only to have their grievances heard, considered and decided.
Nevertheless, the Applicants maintain the judicial review process is an ineffective
mechanism for challenging the Orders because the petitioners were limited in
the record they were allowed to put before the Court.  The submissions of
counsel regarding a ‘catch 22’ wherein the petitioners were unable to obtain a
ruling on the Orders alleged to have been violated (as opposed to a review of
the reconsideration decision) stands in mystifying incongruity with the fact
that at the behest of the petitioners, the reviewing Court acquiesced to their
request to do just that.

[
41
]

There were indeed legal
principles applied in the judicial review that led to certain evidence being
excluded from the record, but to suggest this Court could find that the
judicial review process as it unfolded in this province’s highest court was
ineffective is tantamount to suggesting that this Court could sit in review of
the Court of Appeal.

[
42
]

I have considered all
of the Applicants’ submissions regarding why I should depart from the reasoning
of the Court
in
Lucier
, and I cannot accede to them.  The Applicants go
on to submit that even if I find
Lucier
to be binding legal authority,
the cases at bar are distinguishable on their facts. The Applicants who were
petitioners in
Beaudoin
, that is Pastor Koopman, Brent Smith, Riverside
Calvary Chapel and Immanuel Covenant Reformed Church, contend that because they
engaged in the reconsideration and judicial review process,
Lucier
is
distinguishable
.  Pastor Lucier did not request a reconsideration or bring a
petition for judicial review.

[
43
]

This submission
misapprehends
the decision in
Lucier
.  The Court’s observation that
Pastor Lucier could have pursued a reconsideration or judicial review is simply
an explanation of what the accused in that case could have done instead of
breaching the Order first and seeking a constitutional remedy later.
The
decision in
Lucier
does not turn on whether the accused pursued the
options that were available to him to challenge the Order.  It turns on the Court’s
conclusion that the legislature did not intend to allow people to attack the
Order at trial, once it had already been breached.  Pastor Lucier’s
Charter

challenge was not dismissed
because
he failed to pursue other remedies.
It was dismissed because the law set out avenues for him to review the Order
instead of bringing a
Charter
challenge at trial.  Whether he took advantage
of those avenues or not is immaterial to the ratio of the case.

[
44
]

The decision in
Lucier

is no less applicable to the Applicants who did seek reconsideration and who
did petition for judicial review.  Their remedies now lie in appealing the
results of that review, which they are in the process of doing.  The Applicants
submit it would be fundamentally unfair to deprive them of a possible defence
in their trials, but this overlooks the fact that it is the obligation of the
courts to respect the intentions of lawmakers.  And if, as here, the
legislature did not intend to allow people a collateral attack on an
administrative order regime, then the courts must respect the will of the legislature,
even if someone’s innocence is at stake.

[
45
]

Nothing presented at
this
Vukelich
hearing persuades me that
Lucier
is not binding on
this Court by virtue of horizontal
stare decisis
.  In addition, I agree
entirely with
the reasoning in
Lucier
, and would adopt its application
of the
Maybrun
analysis to the analogous facts before this Court.  This
would result in the same finding that it is an impermissible collateral attack
to allow for challenges to the Orders in this Court.

Legal Viability

[
46
]

The factual basis I have been invited to consider at the
Vukelich

hearing is set out in an Agreed Statement of Fact and many exhibits.  Both counsel made fulsome submissions and provided a rather enormous
volume of materials, much of which replicates the record before the Courts in
Beaudoin
.
This has been helpful in order to understand very clearly the context in which
those higher court decisions were made.  While the
record before me is voluminous, the position of the Crown is not complex.  The
Crown submits that the constitutional issues raised in these applications has
already been heard and the constitutional validity of the Orders has been
upheld.

[
47
]

At the
Beaudoin
petition
in Supreme Court the petitioners sought a declaration that the following Orders
are unconstitutional breaches of their
ss. 2(a)
(b)(c)(d),
7
and
15 (1)

Charter

rights and are of no force and effect:

“Orders made by
the Public Health Officer entitled "Gatherings and Events" and made
pursuant to
Sections 30
,
31
,
32
and
39(3)

Public Health Act, SBC 2008, c. 28
,
including orders of November 19, 20202, December 2nd, 9th, 15th and 24th, 2020
and such further orders as may be pronounced which prohibit or unduly restrict
gatherings for public protests and for worship and/or other religious
gatherings including services, festivals, ceremonies, receptions, weddings,
funerals, baptisms, celebrations of life and related activities associated with
houses of worship and faith communities”.(
Beaudoin
BCSC para 68)

[
48
]

These are the precise
arguments that all Applicants seek to advance against these same Orders in this
proceeding.  Similarly, in
Beaudoin
the petitioners advanced the
argument that the Orders should be set aside because they are an
ultra vires

extension of the PHOs authority, which has also be argued before me.  It is
relevant for reasons I will detail below, that at the judicial review, the
petitioners also sought an order that their violation tickets, almost all of
which are now before this Court, be dismissed.  All of the above mentioned applications
for relief to the Court in
Beaudoin
were dismissed by the Court, in a
decision later affirmed by the Court of Appeal.

[
49
]

At the judicial review,
Chief Justice Hinkson had before him affidavits from the petitioners and others
regarding their religious beliefs and the efforts being taken in their churches
to prevent the spread of Covid-19.  He also had the communications between the
petitioners and the PHO or her delegates with respect to the impugned Orders up
to and including February 10 2021.  He also considered information regarding
exemptions granted to Orthodox Jewish congregations, which is the basis for
part of the Applicants’ argument before this Court.

[
50
]

What the Court in
Beaudoin

expressly did not admit that has been put before me to consider on this
Vukelich

hearing, is the evidence of Dr.’s Warren and Kettner.  They are experts in
infectious diseases and public health, preventative medicine and general
surgery.  Dr. Warren provides estimates of risk in the Canadian epidemiologic
summary and opinions regarding the risk of transmission of Covid-19 at in
person worship services in B.C. relative to other activities permitted under
the provincial health orders.  Dr. Kettner responded to evidence of the PHOs
delegate, Dr. Emerson and provided his opinion about the transmission risk of
the petitioners’ worship services compared to other permitted gatherings.

[
51
]

The Applicants’
position that
Beaudoin
is not determinative of their
Charter

challenges rests on the following arguments.  First, they submit rulings made
in the context of a judicial review are not binding in the criminal context.
Second, they argue the ruling in
Beaudoin
does not represent a
declaration of validity that would also apply to Pastors Champ and Butler who
were not parties in
Beaudoin
.  Finally, they submit the alleged breaches
with respect to
ss.7
and 15 were not ruled on in
Beaudoin
.

Is a
Decision on Judicial Review Binding?

[
52
]

I cannot accept the
Applicants’ submission that this Court would not be bound to follow the ruling
in
Beaudoin
that the Orders are constitutionally valid.  The Applicants
have advanced no authority to support their contention that constitutional
challenges made in administrative law proceedings are not binding in criminal
cases.  Weighing heavily against this reasoning is a body of civil
jurisprudence routinely cited as precedent in criminal cases.  Crown has
provided several examples in their written submissions:
Suresh v. Canada
(Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)
,
2002 SCC 1 (CanLII)
,
[2002] 1 S.C.R. 3
;
Sierra
Club of Canada v. Canada (Minister of Finance)
,
2002 SCC 41 (CanLII)
,
[2002] 2 S.C.R. 522
;
Saskatchewan
(Human Rights Commission) v. Whatcott
,
2013 SCC 11
;
Ktunaxa Nation v.
British Columbia (Forests, Lands and Natural Resource Operations)
,
2017 SCC 54 (CanLII)
,
[2017] 2
S.C.R. 386
.

[
53
]

Counsel for the
Applicants submits that it makes no sense for a ruling on judicial review to
bind this Court when the evidence and legal tests will be different.  With
respect to evidence, the Applicants intend to adduce medical opinions from Dr.
Kettner and Dr. Warren, a newspaper article, and statements made by the PHO in
a subsequent book that purportedly impugn the accuracy and reliability of the evidentiary
foundation for the
Beaudoin
decision.

[
54
]

The Applicants submit this additional evidence is essential to the
s.1 analysis and that with the benefit of this evidence, this Court could
conceivably come to a different conclusion than the Court of Appeal.  This
argument must fail.  It is not open to lower courts to revisit binding rulings
about constitutional validity absent a fundamental shift in the legal or
factual matrix.  See
Canada
(Attorney General) v. Bedford
,
2013 SCC 72

at para
38-47
and
Carter v.
Canada (Attorney General),

2015 SCC 5
.

[
55
]

The standard for
revisiting such precedent is high, lower courts are not entitled to ignore
binding precedent.  For example, even something as significant as the advent of
the internet did not warrant revisiting constitutional rulings of the Supreme
Court of Canada regarding hate speech and freedom of expression (
R. v. Topham

2017 BCSC 259

para
72-81
).  The balance
struck by
the test set out in
Bedford
is between the need for the law to
grow when new issues arise or evidence fundamentally shifts the parameters of
the debate, and on the other hand the need for finality and stability to
maintain the rule of law (at para 44).

[
56
]

It is important in this
analysis to be clear about what is new or different in these applications
compared to the review in
Beaudoin
.  In the cases before me, even for
the Applicants who were not petitioners in
Beaudoin
, I have been presented
with nothing that would distinguish the alleged breaches from what was
considered by our Court of Appeal.  I pause to note that the applications
before me make reference to the Orders being
ultra vires
.  Counsel has
clarified at this hearing that this argument is subsumed by the
Charter

applications.  In other words, if the court were to find that that the Orders
are unconstitutional then it must be outside the scope of the PHOs authority to
make them.  This mirrors the argument made in
Beaudoin
.  As was the case
in
Beaudoin
, there is no challenge to the PHA provisions giving Dr.
Henry the power to make the Orders (BCCA at para 129).

[
57
]

It bears repeating that
the nature of the alleged breaches are identical to those in
Beaudoin
.  This
is a critical point to grasp in order to understand why it is not open to this Court
to come to any other conclusion than the Court of Appeal regarding the
constitutional validity of the Orders.  Despite emphasizing the individual
nature of
Charter
infringements in submissions, the Applicants have not
pointed to any factual basis to find the breaches are materially different than
in
Beaudoin
.  The additional evidence they would put before this Court
supports the contention, advanced by all Applicants, that the Crown cannot
justify the
Charter
infringements under
s.1
.

[
58
]

I have reviewed the
evidence the Applicants have submitted that was not before the Court in
Beaudoin
.
It is incapable of meeting the standard of a ‘fundamental shift’ in the legal
or factual landscape that would allow a lower court to depart from precedent
established by the Court of Appeal just one year ago.  The newspaper article
and excerpts from Dr. Henry’s book, even if accepted as true, could not sustain
the kind of weight the Applicants ascribe to them.  The newspaper article
regarding actual incidents of Covid-19 infection having a higher variable range
than data relied on by the PHO at the time the Orders were made, does not
advance the Applicants’ position that the Orders were irrational arbitrary and
discriminatory.  If anything it tends to emphasize the degree of the emergency
that needed to be addressed with public health orders.  And in any event, as
the Court of Appeal observed when reviewing the decisions of the PHO in the s.1
analysis there is no room for hindsight (
Beaudoin
BCCA, para 268).
Similarly, the excerpts from Dr. Henry’s book do not amount to an admission
that her Orders were untethered to the objectives in the PHA.

[
59
]

The evidence the
Applicants’ most want this Court to consider, and I have, are the affidavits of
Dr.’s Kettner and Warren.  This evidence was also reviewed at both levels of
court in
Beaudoin
.  While the affidavits were not formally considered Chief
Justice Hinkson said the following at paragraphs 117-118, 121-125:

117
In
comparing the risk of worship services compared to other permitted activities,
Dr. Kettner extrapolated the frequency of church attendances in B.C. from a
2003 Statistics Canada report. In doing so, he incorrectly understood that one
of the rules of the Free Reformed Church of Chilliwack was to exclude people
over the age of 65 from attendance. He was also not apparently provided with,
or alternatively chose not to comment on the practices of the other two
religious petitioner churches.

118
Dr. Henry did not have the reports of these two doctors available
to her when she made the impugned G&E Orders. As I have indicated above, if
I allowed the religious petitioners to rely upon this
purportedly
expert
evidence, that would permit them to bypass the statutory decision maker without
affording deference to Dr. Henry's findings on the face of the record before
her.[emphasis added]

Later at
paragraph 121 the Court cites Brossard J.
in
Nencioni v. Mailloux
,

1984 CanLII 2739 (QC CS)
,
[1985] R.L. 532 (Sup. Ct.)
, at p. 548
:

[TRANSLATION] ... it is not for the court to
choose between two schools of scientific thought which seem to be equally
reasonable and are founded on scientific writings and texts ...

122
The
petitioners contend that as their proceeding is primarily centered on what is
in substance a
Charter
challenge to Dr. Henry's G&E Orders, as
opposed to the judicial review of an administrative decision, no deference is
owed to Dr. Henry in determining the constitutionality of her orders. They say
that a standard of correctness should be applied.

123
I am
unable to accept this over-simplification. I accept that insofar as the
Charter

is concerned, Dr. Henry's orders must reflect and incorporate
Charter

values, but so long as they do, the impugned orders are in areas of science and
medicine.

124
In the
areas of science and medicine, Dr. Henry is entitled to deference and the
appropriate standard of review of such matters is that of reasonableness.

125

Even if the opinions of Dr. Warren and Dr. Kettner were
admissible, they represent, at best, an alternate view of the risks that have
been considered and weighed by Dr. Henry. They do not persuade me that her
conclusions and G&E Orders are unreasonable
.  [emphasis added]

[
60
]

The Applicants maintain
before me that the court’s dismissive comments regarding the utility of these
opinions are to be expected given the deference that was owed to the PHO, that
would not be owed to her under the
Oakes
analysis.  It is simply not
true that this Court in an
Oakes
analysis would owe no deference to Dr.
Henry if alternate views of the risks were put forward.  This Court would still
be deciding whether the Orders fell within a range of reasonable alternatives,
not whether with the benefit of hindsight a less restrictive approach could
have been taken (
Beaudoin
BCCA para 278, 290, 301).

[
61
]

The Court of Appeal
explains:

legislators and
decision makers are afforded a level of deference, or margin of appreciation,
under both a reasonableness review and in applying the
Oakes
framework.
The width of the margin takes its meaning from context. The context that
existed when the impugned orders were made was singular in its complexity. The
PHO was required to make real-time decisions that proportionately balanced

Charter
protections with the protection of the public in a time of crisis.
Failure to adopt rights-limiting, protective measures in the face of a known
and unacceptable risk of transmission arising from faith-based gatherings would
likely result in a preventable loss of life.   A conclusion, based on the
clarity that only hindsight brings, that the orders made by the PHO were not
reasonable because the same objective might have been achieved by easing,
however slightly, the limitations then in place would take the analysis in a
case like this to an impractical extreme (para 278).

[
62
]

I am not suggesting
that the affidavits of Dr’s Kettner and Warren formed part of the record on
which the judicial review was decided.  They did not.  What is determinative of
this issue, however, is the fact that despite having full knowledge that this
evidence existed, the Court of Appeal decided it was able to undertake an analysis
of whether the violations of the same
Charter
rights alleged here could
be justified in a free and democratic society using the
Oakes
analysis, and
did so, finding that the Orders were not arbitrary, disproportionate, or overly
broad on the same standard the Applicants intend to argue here.

[
63
]

The Applicants also take
the position that the decisions in
Beaudoin
reveal that the
constitutional rulings were not intended to be determinative of the
petitioners’ tickets, or to curtail their ability to bring the
Charter

applications that the Crown now seeks to summarily dismiss.  In particular the
Applicants point to portions of both
Beaudoin
decisions where the Courts
refer to the fact that the petitioners can challenge their tickets in
provincial court.  In my view, the passages highlighted by the Applicants show
both courts delineating the scope of their rulings.  On judicial review and
appeal, the courts could rule on the constitutionality of the Orders, but they
could not and would not displace the function of the lower courts to resolve
the tickets.  This becomes more clear in the full context of the submissions
referred to by Crown counsel.

[
64
]

I do not read the
excerpts highlighted by the Applicants as detracting in any way from the
binding effect of the courts’ rulings when it comes to the constitutional
validity of the Orders.  Particularly when one considers the Court of Appeal’s
willingness to engage the
Oakes
analysis to guide the trial courts on a
novel issue of pressing importance to many.  The Applicants have not been
prevented from raising
Charter
challenges.  It is open to them to do so, they
have done so, and this Court can resolve them, either summarily or following a
full evidentiary hearing.  It is also trite to say that with respect to all
tickets save the one that has already been tried, the accused are presumed
innocent and can challenge the tickets in any number of other ways.

[
65
]

The Applicants also take the position this Court could arrive at a
different conclusion in an
Oakes
s.1 analysis because this aspect of the

Beaudoin
decision is non-binding
obiter dicta
.  I cannot accede
to this submission.  The
Oakes
analysis by the Court of Appeal is intentional
and complete.  In fact, the Justice Fitch re-framed the grounds of appeal to be
decided by the Court in order to reflect the arguments being made by the
petitioners, such that an issue to be decided on the appeal was whether the
Orders were “unjustified under the
Oakes
analysis or, in the
alternative, unreasonable under
Doré
?”(para 138).  In resolving this
issue the Court undertook a thorough and independent alternate s.1 analysis and
then applied it to the circumstances of the case before them.  In my view this
reasoning easily falls within the “wider circle of analysis which is obviously
intended for guidance and which should be accepted as authoritative.”
R. v. Henry
,
2005 SCC 76
(para
57
).

[
66
]

It cannot be forgotten
that the ultimate issue at this hearing is whether there is any reasonable prospect
that the constitutional challenges brought by the Applicants could succeed.
The Applicants have no legal authority to support their contention that this Court
could come to a different conclusion in a s.1
Oakes
analysis.  Higher
court rulings from across the country, including those that employ the
Oakes

analysis for similar breaches, have all found that that
Charter
infringements
are justified under s.1 (
Ontario v. Trinity Bible Chapel
et al
2022 ONSC
1344
,
Gateway Bible Baptist Church et al v. Manitoba et al

2021 MBQB 219

and
Taylor v. Newfoundland and Labrador

2020 NLSC 125
).

[
67
]

I have also considered
that some of the tickets before me involve alleged violations of Orders that
were not considered by the court in
Beaudoin
because they post-date the judicial
review.  I find the Applicants remain without any reasonable possibility of
success in these challenges, given these Orders fall squarely within the class
of orders the petitioners identified for the review in
Beaudoin
.

[
68
]

In conclusion, I find
that the decision in
Beaudoin
would be determinative of the
constitutional challenges.  The findings the Applicants ask this Court to make
following a full evidentiary hearing would be inconsistent with binding
precedent.

Is Beaudoin
Binding on Non-Petitioners?

[
69
]

Beaudoin
is also determinative of the
constitutional challenges raised by Pastors Champ and Butler, who were not
petitioners in the
Beaudoin
decision.  The scope of the
Beaudoin

decision applies to any person who is charged under the Orders reviewed by the Court
in
Beaudoin
, and who is alleging the same kind of constitutional
violations to their right to gather in person for worship.  I have been
directed to no evidence that would suggest the challenges brought by Pastors
Champ and Butler are distinguishable.

Is Beaudoin
Determinative of the ss.7 and 15 applications?

[
70
]

The Applicants have
framed their ss. 7 and 15 applications on these tickets just as the petitioners
did in
Beaudoin
.  The decisions at both levels of court in
Beaudoin

reflect the fact that the Applicants’ ss.7 and 15 applications are subsumed by
their applications under
s.2
.  Chief Justice Hinkson said the following about
the s.7 breach alleged in
Beaudoin
:

186
Moreover,
given the concessions of the respondents and my findings with respect to the
religious petitioners’
s. 2

Charter

rights, I find that it is
unnecessary to expand the jurisprudence relating to
s. 7
of the
Charter
,
and will make no finding with respect to s. 7.

187
Likewise, here the religious petitioners focussed their submissions
on their
s. 2

Charter

rights, and addressed their claim pursuant to
s. 7

of the
Charter
in only a summary way.

[
71
]

With respect to the alleged
s.15(1)
breach, the Court found there
was no evidence that the Orders only disadvantage a group of people based on
their religious beliefs.  At paragraph 191 the Court notes that:

The same activities are allowed and
restricted for secular and religious people, and whether in a secular or
religious setting. The respondents point out that religious schools are as open
as secular ones. Funerals can be conducted by any religious or secular
community. Unless they are covered by a specific exemption, non-religious
people have no more ability to gather than religious ones.

192
The G&E Orders are also not an absolute prohibition on
in-person religious gatherings. The current orders permit multiple forms of in-person
religious gatherings: …

[
72
]

I also note the petitioners in
Beaudoin
drew the Court’s
attention to the same evidence regarding reconsideration requests made by the synagogues.
Ultimately the Court decided that it need not make a finding with respect to
s.15 because of the summary way in which the petitioners pursued this claim.

[
73
]

However the Court of Appeal has foreclosed any argument the
Applicants could revive in these cases.  In finding that regardless of a s.15
breach being established the Court opines: “
I can
identify no analytical route that could conceivably lead to a different
application of the proportionality analysis if, in addition to the
s. 2

breaches, the orders were also found to have violated s. 15 (
Beaudoin
,
BCCA para 234).”  The Court further decided that breaches of more sections
would not change the s.1 analysis (
Beaudoin
, BCCA para 234, 238).

[
74
]

On appeal the petitioners did not pursue or seek additional rulings
beyond the breaches of
ss.2
and 15.  In determining that the Order could be justified
under s.1, the Court of Appeal took into account the same arguments under ss.7
and 15 that the Applicants wish to advance on these tickets.  As such, the
ultimate decision regarding constitutional validity in
Beaudoin
is
determinative on all alleged breaches before this Court.

Conclusion

[
75
]

In the
Beaudoin

petition Chief Justice Hinkson concluded that:

Although the impacts of the G&E Orders
on the religious petitioners’ rights are significant, the benefits to the
objectives of the orders are even more so. In my view, the orders represent a
reasonable and proportionate balance.

Thus, the
respondents have proven that the limits the G&E Orders place on the
religious petitioners’
s. 2

Charter
rights are justified under
s. 1
of the
Charter.  (
Beaudoin
, para 247-248)

[
76
]

In doing so the Court
rejected the position of the Applicants before me who said then and say now
that the Orders were arbitrary, irrational or disproportionate because worship
services were prohibited when other types of transactional gatherings were
allowed.  This reasoning was upheld by the Court of Appeal on the basis of the
Doré
analysis
applied in the decision under review, and also on the basis of the
Oakes

test that could be applied in this Court.

[
77
]

The Applicants submit
there is no absolute rule against re-litigating the very issues decided in
Beaudoin
.
This is the very crux of the issue when it comes to the legal viability of
their
Charter
applications.  It is true that the rule is not absolute, it
is subject to review where the legal or factual matrix has fundamentally
changed.  But until then it is important to recognize that
stare decisis

is one of the pillars on which our common law system is built.  It is not a
principle that thwarts justice, but rather promotes and upholds the rule of law
by essentially providing citizens with law that is predictable and uniform.  It
“elevates the rule of law over above the rule of individual judges.”
R. v.
Hummel
,
1987 CanLII 4075
(ONSC)
.

[
78
]

In conclusion, I find
that the
Charter
applications are without merit because they are
inconsistent with binding precedent and because there is no reasonable
possibility of success based on existing law.  I have also found the
applications are impermissible collateral attacks on the Orders and should be
summarily dismissed for that reason as well.  I have not ruled on Crown’s
argument that the applications are also collateral attacks on the
Beaudoin

proceeding, however I need not given my other findings.

[
79
]

All
Charter

Applications subject to this
Vukelich
hearing are summarily dismissed.
